title: Polluter Pays Principle and Absolute Liability

content.overview: The polluter-pays principle requires the polluter to bear the cost of preventing, controlling and remedying environmental harm. In Indian environmental jurisprudence it is paired with absolute liability for hazardous or inherently dangerous activity: the enterprise owes a non-delegable duty to the community and cannot rely on the traditional exceptions to strict liability. Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum treated polluter-pays and the precautionary principle as part of Indian environmental law.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Who caused the harm? (2) Remediation and compensation cost on the polluter? (3) Hazardous activity — absolute liability? (4) Distinguish from public trust and precaution alone?
content.study:
Polluter pays is a cost-allocation principle; absolute liability is a liability standard for hazardous enterprise. They often travel together in environmental orders but answer different questions.

Cases already in migrated file (retained, not invented): Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) 5 SCC 647; M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (1987) 1 SCC 395 (absolute liability); M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997) 1 SCC 388 (public trust — distinguish).

sections.heading: Polluter pays
sections.body: The polluter bears the cost of prevention, control and remediation of environmental damage caused by the activity.

sections.heading: Absolute liability
sections.body: Enterprise engaged in hazardous or inherently dangerous activity owes an absolute and non-delegable duty; traditional strict-liability exceptions do not apply.

sections.heading: Vellore holding
sections.body: Precautionary principle and polluter-pays principle form part of Indian environmental law and inform judicial and administrative action.

sections.heading: Remedies
sections.body: Compensation, remediation directions, closure or compliance orders through NGT, High Court or Supreme Court as the cause allows.

sections.heading: Distinctions
sections.body: Public trust (State as trustee of commons) and precaution (act despite scientific uncertainty) are related but distinct doctrines.

examples.title: Industrial pollution
examples.body: Tannery discharge contaminates water and soil — polluter directed to remediate and compensate under polluter-pays; absolute liability may apply if the activity is hazardous.

hypotheticals.question: Can a hazardous industry plead Act of God to escape environmental liability?
hypotheticals.analysis: Under absolute liability as developed in M.C. Mehta, traditional strict-liability exceptions do not apply to hazardous enterprise.

distinctions.title: Polluter pays vs public trust
distinctions.left: Cost and liability on the polluter/enterprise.
distinctions.right: State holds natural resources in trust for the public.

misconceptions.trap: Polluter pays and absolute liability are the same rule.
misconceptions.correction: Polluter pays allocates cost; absolute liability is a standard of duty for hazardous activity.

cases.name: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India
cases.ratioDecidendi: The precautionary principle and polluter-pays principle are part of Indian environmental law and must inform judicial and administrative action.
cases.holding: Directed remediation and compliance with environmental principles.
cases.relevance: Lead authority for polluter pays in India.

cases.name: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India
cases.ratioDecidendi: An enterprise engaged in hazardous or inherently dangerous activity owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community and cannot rely on the traditional exceptions to strict liability.
